Hackers breach govt webmail while running parallel crypto fraud

China-linked Jewelbug breached shared government webmail infrastructure in the Middle East to steal cookies, credentials, and emails across 15 tenants, while Symantec found the same operators also ran large-scale cryptocurrency fraud from the same control panel.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The Jewelbug hacker group compromised webmail accounts belonging to 15 government tenants in a campaign targeting a country in the Middle East.
  • 02Symantec found that Jewelbug’s espionage campaign and cryptocurrency fraud operations were conducted from the same control panel.
  • 03Jewelbug gained write access to a shared webmail installation and inserted a malicious script into a common template, causing it to run on login pages and mailbox views across the affected tenants.
  • 04The script exfiltrated webmail cookies and checked whether users belonged to targeted government domains before showing valuable targets a fake Adobe Flash update prompt that installed the Antino backdoor and browser tooling.
  • 05Symantec said Jewelbug’s victim database contained more than one million implant check-in rows, over 580,000 stolen browser cookies, several thousand captured credentials, and more than 2,300 exfiltrated email bodies.

The Jewelbug hacker group has been conducting espionage operations against governments, militaries, and critical-sector organizations while also running cryptocurrency fraud. In a recent campaign targeting a country in the Middle East, the group compromised webmail accounts belonging to 15 government tenants. Symantec found that the espionage campaign and cryptocurrency fraud were conducted from the same control panel.

Jewelbug gained write access to a shared webmail installation and inserted a malicious script into a common template, causing it to run on login pages and mailbox views across affected tenants. The script opened a WebSocket connection to the attackers’ command-and-control server, stole webmail cookies, and checked whether the user’s email address belonged to a targeted government domain. Valuable targets were shown a fake Adobe Flash update prompt that installed the Antino backdoor and browser tooling.

Symantec said Jewelbug’s victim database contained more than one million implant check-in rows, over 580,000 stolen browser cookies, several thousand captured credentials, and more than 2,300 exfiltrated email bodies. The group also used tools including XG-Web, a malicious browser extension named PDF Viewer, and a Rust-based implant called ClientKing. Its cryptocurrency fraud operation used AI-generated articles, fake crypto exchange sites, lookalike domains impersonating OKX and Binance, and click-fraud bots to drive traffic and manipulate search rankings.

  • A single script tag placed in a shared webmail template allowed Jewelbug to reach users across more than 15 government webmail tenants, showing how compromise of a common platform can multiply impact across many agencies.
  • Jewelbug’s script did not treat every webmail user the same; it checked whether the user’s email address belonged to targeted government domains before delivering the fake Adobe Flash update prompt to valuable targets.
  • Symantec linked espionage and cryptocurrency fraud to the same control panel, indicating that Jewelbug’s intelligence collection and profit-driven scams were operationally intertwined rather than isolated activities.
  • Jewelbug used public Google Docs to host obfuscated payloads retrieved and executed by its implants, helping its traffic blend in with legitimate Google services.
  • The group’s cryptocurrency fraud operation combined AI-generated fake download pages, lookalike domains impersonating OKX and Binance, and click-fraud bots to drive victims toward fraudulent sites.

A China-based hacker group called Jewelbug broke into shared government webmail used by 15 government tenants in a Middle Eastern country, allowing it to steal login data, browser cookies, and emails from targeted users. The same group was also running a large cryptocurrency fraud operation, using fake exchange sites and other scams to make money. This matters because the victims included government, military, telecom, education, aviation, and other critical organizations across the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and South Asia, showing how one group can mix spying on sensitive institutions with large-scale financial crime.

AI 'watermark removers' flood the web. Almost none can prove they work.

A wave of tools claiming to remove Claude and other AI text watermarks has appeared, but most cannot prove they work because Anthropic has not released its detector or technical details. The verifiable parts mainly strip metadata or hidden characters, while the real watermark is embedded in word choices and likely requires heavy rewriting.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A market for AI watermark removal tools appeared days after Anthropic disclosed that it had enabled invisible marks in everything Claude writes.
  • 02The claims that these tools can defeat Anthropic's text watermark cannot currently be verified because Anthropic has not published how the watermark works or released a detector.
  • 03Some tools can verifiably remove hidden characters and file metadata such as C2PA, EXIF, and XMP, but the article says Claude's watermark is embedded in word choices rather than hidden characters.
  • 04Guillaume Meyer stated that his watermarks-remover tool removes metadata only for now and does not yet strip the actual text watermark.
  • 05The article warns that tools wired directly into agent pipelines and used to process documents create a supply chain surface, especially in a market where buyers cannot verify claims.

A market for AI watermark removal tools appeared days after Anthropic disclosed that it had enabled invisible marks in everything Claude writes. The tools include a GitHub project with more than 4,500 stars, several newly registered web tools, and services that claim to evade AI detection. The article says none of the claims about defeating Anthropic’s text watermark can currently be checked because Anthropic has not published how the watermark works or released a detector.

The article distinguishes between easy-to-verify cleanup and the harder problem of removing the actual watermark. Tools can strip hidden characters and file metadata such as C2PA, EXIF, and XMP, but Claude’s watermark is described as living in the model’s word choices rather than in hidden characters. Guillaume Meyer, developer of the watermarks-remover project, said his tool currently removes metadata only, while commercial sites make broader claims that the article says are not verifiable against Anthropic’s watermark.

Anthropic says the marking is tied to EU AI Act Article 50 transparency rules and applies to text from models launched on or after August 2, 2026, across Claude services and cloud platforms. A detected mark means content was processed by Claude, not necessarily written by it, and Anthropic says marks can disappear through heavy editing, paraphrasing, or translation. The article warns that watermark-removal tools installed into agent workflows and used to process documents create a supply chain surface, especially in a market where buyers cannot verify whether the tools work.

  • The easiest “removal” wins advertised by some tools are weak evidence, because file metadata can already disappear through ordinary actions like re-saving, converting formats, or taking screenshots.
  • A detected Claude mark may be misleading in practice, because Anthropic says it shows content was processed by Claude and does not prove Claude originally wrote it.
  • Ordinary AI detector scores are not valid proof that a tool removed Anthropic’s watermark, because the article says no public Anthropic watermark detector exists yet.
  • The article highlights agent skills as a concrete risk area, because users may install unvetted watermark-removal code directly into local agent workflows and then route documents through it.
  • Even open-source watermark-removal projects may not perform as advertised, as independent code review found one popular cleaner failed to remove a common hidden-payload technique.

After Anthropic began adding invisible marks to text written or processed by Claude, many websites and code projects quickly appeared claiming they can remove those marks. The article says most of these claims cannot be checked yet, because Anthropic has not published the details or a public way to test whether a mark is still there. This affects people and organizations using Claude, as well as anyone relying on these marks to tell whether text came through an AI system, and it matters because users may trust unproven tools that handle their documents and could create new safety and privacy risks.

Ukraine shuts down 94 fraudulent call centers, seize millions in cash

Ukrainian authorities shut down 94 fraudulent call centers that ran investment, banking, and recovery scams targeting victims in Ukraine and the EU. Police seized millions in cash, crypto wallet access tools, devices, SIM cards, vehicles, and gold, and named 26 suspects.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Ukrainian authorities shut down 94 fraudulent call centers after 411 searches conducted with involvement from the National Police, Ukraine's Security Service, the Prosecutor General’s Office, and German police.
  • 02The call centers posed as bankers, brokers, and law enforcement officers to lure victims into fake investment platforms, obtain bank account access, or pressure them over supposedly suspicious bank transactions.
  • 03Some call centers targeted citizens in foreign countries, particularly in the European Union, and persuaded victims to install remote-access software on their computers.
  • 04Police seized 1,794 fully equipped workstations, 3,336 pieces of computer equipment, 1,346 phones, 5,200 SIM cards, 90 bank cards, access tools for 20 cryptocurrency wallets, 22 vehicles, cash, and gold.
  • 05Authorities have formally notified 26 individuals that they are suspects, and forensic examination of seized equipment is underway to identify victims, losses, organizers, participants, money mules, and money launderers.

Authorities in Ukraine shut down 94 fraudulent call centers across the country that lured people into investment scams or tried to obtain access to bank accounts. The operation took place this week and included 411 searches conducted after an investigation involving the National Police, Ukraine’s Security Service, the Prosecutor General’s Office, and German police. Police said the call centers posed as bankers, brokers, and law enforcement officers to trick victims.

The schemes included fake investment platforms, bank impersonation calls about supposedly suspicious transactions, loan applications, and requests for payment card details. Some victims were persuaded to install remote-access tools on phones and computers, while others were promised help recovering money they had already lost and were scammed again. Police also said some call centers promoted products as medical treatments despite the products having no actual medicinal properties.

During the raids, police seized 1,794 fully equipped workstations, 3,336 pieces of computer equipment, 1,346 phones, 5,200 SIM cards, 90 bank cards, access tools for 20 cryptocurrency wallets, 22 vehicles, cash, and gold. Authorities said 26 individuals have been formally notified that they are suspects. Forensic examination of the seized equipment is underway to identify victims, determine losses, and collect evidence against organizers, participants, money mules, and money launderers.

  • The fraud operation was not limited to one script or audience; police said the call centers ran multiple scam types, including fake investments, bank impersonation, recovery scams, and false medical-treatment sales.
  • The seizure of 5,200 SIM cards alongside 1,346 phones suggests the call centers relied heavily on large-scale phone-based outreach rather than isolated individual scammers.
  • Police said some call centers had dedicated teams for identifying people genuinely interested in investing, showing that victims were being filtered and targeted rather than contacted only at random.
  • The investigation is aimed beyond the call center operators, as police said forensic analysis may identify organizers, money mules, and money launderers connected to the schemes.

Police in Ukraine shut down 94 scam call centers that pretended to be bankers, brokers, or law enforcement officers to trick people out of money or get into their bank accounts. The victims included people in Ukraine and other countries, especially in the European Union, who were pushed into fake investments, loans, remote access to their devices, or bogus help recovering money they had already lost. Authorities seized large amounts of cash, computers, phones, SIM cards, vehicles, gold, and access to cryptocurrency wallets, and 26 people have been named as suspects. This matters because these scams can drain real people’s savings, and the investigation may uncover more victims and others who helped move or hide the stolen money.

White House taps security firms for offensive hack-back operations

A new White House memo directs the National Coordination Center to create a program allowing vetted private security firms to conduct government-approved offensive cyber operations against foreign cybercrime groups. The program marks a major expansion of private-sector involvement in U.S. hack-back efforts, with legal compliance rules, oversight, and financial penalties for violations.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A new White House national security presidential memorandum signed by President Donald Trump directs the National Coordination Center to establish a program allowing private security companies to seek approval to hack foreign cybercrime organizations.
  • 02The program will let the National Coordination Center leverage private-sector capabilities to conduct cyber operations against transnational criminal organizations under U.S. government control and authority.
  • 03Participating security firms will be vetted before entering contracts with the Justice Department or the Department of Homeland Security, and the program will be overseen by executive directors from those departments.
  • 04Companies in the program must maintain a bond or escrow of at least $1 million that can be forfeited if they do not comply with contractual agreements.
  • 05The White House said the program is intended to disrupt foreign criminal organizations involved in ransomware attacks, phishing campaigns, financial fraud, sextortion schemes, and impersonation scams.

A new White House national security presidential memorandum signed by U.S. President Donald Trump directs the National Coordination Center to establish a program for private security companies to seek approval to hack foreign cybercrime organizations. The NCC, which is part of the Homeland Security Task Force, would use private-sector capabilities to conduct cyber operations against transnational criminal organizations under U.S. government control and authority. The White House said the program is aimed at groups involved in ransomware attacks, phishing campaigns, financial fraud, sextortion schemes, and impersonation scams.

The memorandum calls for rigorous procedures for reviewing and conducting these limited cyber operations, with requirements for compliance with the U.S. Constitution, federal law, and applicable international agreements. The program will be overseen by executive directors designated by the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security, and participating companies will be vetted before entering into contracts with one of those departments. Companies must also maintain a bond or escrow of at least $1 million that can be forfeited if they fail to comply with contractual agreements.

Participating firms must immediately stop operations and notify the National Coordination Center if they discover activity that exceeds approved limits, including unintended targeting of U.S. citizens or U.S.-based systems. The White House said U.S. consumers reported losing more than $20.8 billion to cyber-enabled crime in 2025. Veracode co-founder Chris Wysopal described the memo as a major shift in U.S. cyber policy, while former Cyber National Mission Force leader and Automox CTO Jason Kikta called it “a perpetual motion machine for billable threats.”

  • The memo does not create a free-form private hack-back system; participating companies would operate under U.S. government direction, contracts, vetting, and procedures tied to legal and international obligations.
  • The required $1 million bond or escrow creates a direct financial penalty mechanism for companies that fail to follow the program’s contractual rules.
  • The program encourages private companies to coordinate with other private entities and federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies before proposing cyber operations, making threat information sharing part of the operational model.
  • The requirement to immediately stop and notify the National Coordination Center if operations exceed approved limits shows that unintended contact with U.S. citizens or U.S.-based systems is an explicitly anticipated risk.
  • Security experts quoted in the article described the memo as a major policy shift and raised concern that it could create ongoing incentives around billable cyber threats.

The White House signed a memo telling the National Coordination Center to set up a program where approved private security companies can help the U.S. government go after foreign online crime groups. These groups are linked to crimes like ransomware, phishing, financial fraud, sextortion, and impersonation scams, which U.S. consumers reported losing more than $20.8 billion to in 2025. The change matters because it gives private companies a much bigger role in government-directed offensive online operations, with rules meant to keep them within U.S. law and international obligations.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This reports a specific White House policy action that could significantly expand private-sector involvement in government-directed offensive cyber operations. It is broadly relevant to security professionals because it may affect legal, operational, and threat-intelligence practices, but it is not an immediate exploitation or breach event.

Trezor discloses data breach affecting nearly 14,000 customers

Trezor says nearly 14,000 customers had order details exposed after shipping partner ShipMonk was breached through a Metabase zero-day, but Trezor’s own systems and hardware wallets were not compromised. Affected customers should watch for targeted phishing using leaked names, emails, phone numbers, and addresses.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Trezor disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 14,000 customers after its shipping and logistics provider ShipMonk was hacked.
  • 02The exposed order data included full names, shipping addresses, email addresses, and phone numbers for some customers, while others had names, cities, and email addresses exposed.
  • 03The breach affected customers from the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Colombia, Brazil, Italy, and Portugal who received orders between May 10 and August 8, 2026.
  • 04Trezor said its own systems were not compromised, its operations and services were not impacted, and all Trezor devices remain secure.
  • 05ShipMonk told affected customers that attackers exploited a vulnerability in the third-party analytics platform Metabase to access customer-related data.

Trezor disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 14,000 customers after ShipMonk, its shipping and logistics provider, was hacked. Attackers accessed customer order data, including full names, shipping addresses, email addresses, and phone numbers. The breach affects customers in the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Colombia, Brazil, Italy, and Portugal who received orders between May 10 and August 8, 2026.

Trezor said 11,742 customers had full exposure of name, email, phone number, and shipping address, while 1,947 customers had partial exposure of name, city, and email. The company said its own systems were not compromised, its operations and services were not impacted, and all Trezor devices remain secure. Trezor warned affected customers that the exposed data could be used for more sophisticated phishing attempts, including fake emails, phone calls, letters, or impersonation of banks, crypto exchanges, or Trezor.

ShipMonk told affected customers that attackers exploited a vulnerability in the third-party analytics platform Metabase to access data related to their account and customers. Metabase had previously revealed that threat actors exploited a critical SQL injection zero-day vulnerability to gain administrator access to customer instances and steal data. BleepingComputer reported that Framework and Tally also notified customers after their Metabase instances were hijacked, and it learned that ShipMonk received extortion emails from the ShinyHunters extortion gang.

  • The breach creates a high-risk phishing scenario because attackers have enough personal order details to make fake emails, phone calls, and letters appear credible to Trezor customers.
  • The incident shows that customer data exposure can come through a chain of third parties, as Trezor customers were affected through ShipMonk and ShipMonk attributed the access to Metabase software.
  • Metabase-related data theft was not limited to ShipMonk, since Framework and Tally also notified customers after their Metabase instances were hijacked.
  • ShipMonk told customers that Metabase had patched the vulnerability and invalidated active sessions, indicating the response included both a software fix and session reset.
  • BleepingComputer learned that ShipMonk received extortion emails from the ShinyHunters extortion gang, adding an extortion element to the incident.

Trezor said nearly 14,000 customers had order information exposed after its shipping provider, ShipMonk, was hacked. The affected people are customers in the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Colombia, Brazil, Italy, and Portugal who received orders between May 10 and August 8, 2026, and the exposed details included names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, or city information. Trezor says its own systems were not hacked and its devices remain secure, but scammers could use the stolen personal details to send convincing fake emails, calls, or letters pretending to be Trezor, banks, or crypto exchanges.

WhatsApp rolls out new feature that flags potential scam messages

WhatsApp is rolling out an optional Scam Alert feature that uses on-device machine learning to warn users about likely scam messages from non-contacts without sending message content to Meta. Users can block, report, continue, or mark chats as trusted, and the feature can be disabled at any time.
KEY POINTS
  • 01WhatsApp has begun a limited beta rollout of an optional Scam Alert feature that uses an on-device machine learning model to warn users about potential scam messages.
  • 02Scam Alert checks incoming messages from non-contacts for known scam patterns using linguistic signals and probabilistic classification based on conversational structure.
  • 03WhatsApp says no message content leaves the device for classification or is automatically reported to WhatsApp, Meta, or anyone else.
  • 04When Scam Alert detects a possible scam, it shows a chat warning asking the user to block, report, or continue the conversation.
  • 05Users can mark a flagged chat as trusted, disable Scam Alert at any time, and optionally share the last five received messages with WhatsApp to help improve the feature’s accuracy.

WhatsApp has begun rolling out a new optional “Scam Alert” feature in a limited beta. The feature uses an on-device machine learning model to warn users when scammers may be targeting them. WhatsApp is testing the warning system with researchers in its Bug Bounty community.

Scam Alert is designed to check incoming messages from non-contacts against known scam patterns. WhatsApp says it uses linguistic signals and probabilistic classification based on conversational structure, while keeping classification on the user’s device. The company says no message content leaves the device for classification or is automatically reported to WhatsApp, Meta, or anyone else.

When the model detects a potential scam attempt, the user sees a chat warning asking them to block, report, or continue the conversation. If the warning is incorrect, the user can mark the chat as trusted, which removes the warning and prevents Scam Alert from flagging that chat again. WhatsApp says users can disable Scam Alert at any time, and the feature is part of broader efforts to protect its more than 3 billion users from scams and other threats.

  • WhatsApp is trying to balance scam detection with end-to-end encryption by running the scam classifier locally on the user’s device instead of sending message content to Meta for analysis.
  • The feature focuses specifically on messages from non-contacts, which shows WhatsApp is targeting scam conversations before users engage deeply with unfamiliar senders.
  • WhatsApp is testing Scam Alert with researchers in its Bug Bounty community before broader release, indicating the company is treating the feature’s security and reliability as part of the rollout process.
  • User feedback is built into the feature: people can mark a flagged chat as trusted and may choose to share the last five received messages to help improve detection accuracy.

WhatsApp is testing an optional new Scam Alert feature that warns people when a message from someone outside their contacts looks like a possible scam. The check happens on the person’s own phone, and WhatsApp says the message content is not sent to WhatsApp, Meta, or anyone else for the warning. This matters because more than 3 billion people use WhatsApp, and scammers often try to trick users before they realize a conversation is dangerous.

The article argues that AI coding assistants are generating third-party dependency suggestions faster than enterprise security teams and open source maintainers can review them. It focuses on the question of who is vetting AI-generated code and dependencies before they enter software projects. The author says post-commit Software Composition Analysis scans struggle to keep pace when unvetted or hallucinated dependencies are added at machine speed.

A key risk described is “slopsquatting,” where a large language model suggests a package name that does not exist in registries such as PyPI or npm. Attackers can register the hallucinated package name, upload a malicious payload, and wait for developer environments or CI/CD systems to fetch it. The article cites a USENIX Security study of sixteen code-generation models and more than 500,000 code samples, and describes an early-2026 case where a hallucinated npm package name, react-codeshift, spread through forks to more than 230 repositories.

The article says this issue also increases the burden on open source maintainers as AI-generated pull requests arrive with unvetted dependencies and higher defect density. It cites Kusari telemetry showing 85% of organizations use AI coding assistants, while only 9% have dedicated AI AppSec controls. The author recommends controlling dependencies at the point of selection by restricting direct registry fetching, isolating AI-suggested dependencies for analysis, and using a governed ingestion gateway such as ActiveState’s Secure Open Source Library and Curated Catalog.

  • The article frames the main security failure as an intake problem rather than an AI accuracy problem, arguing that even better models would not remove the need to govern what dependencies are allowed into builds.
  • The cited react-codeshift example shows that a hallucinated package name can spread through repository forks before anyone notices that no human intentionally selected it.
  • The article highlights a large governance gap: 85% of organizations use AI coding assistants, but only 9% have dedicated AI AppSec controls.
  • The article argues that post-commit scanning can become ineffective noise when AI-generated code creates alerts faster than engineers can review them.
  • The article presents direct public registry access from developer workstations and AI agents as a specific control point that organizations can restrict to reduce slopsquatting risk.

The article says AI coding tools are suggesting software add-ons so quickly that companies and open source volunteers may not have time to check whether those add-ons are real, safe, or intentionally planted by attackers. Developers, company security teams, and open source maintainers are affected because a fake or unsafe package can be pulled into a project without anyone deliberately choosing it. In the real world, this can lead to compromised software builds, more work for maintainers, and production applications being exposed before the problem is caught.

An Akira ransomware affiliate disabled endpoint detection and response on a compromised system by restarting the machine into Safe Mode with Networking. The attack began on August 4 after the attacker gained access through an exposed SonicWall VPN device that did not have multi-factor authentication. Huntress said the attacker reached the domain controller through RDP, enumerated Active Directory users and computers, then moved to an application server.

The attacker used WinRAR to archive mapped file shares and s5cmd to upload stolen data to an attacker-controlled S3 bucket before installing AnyDesk for remote access. They then used AnyDesk to reboot the host into Safe Mode with Networking, where the Huntress agent and Microsoft Defender real-time protection were disabled. Huntress said that for 10 minutes in Safe Mode, the host had no working EDR and antivirus was blinded.

The attempt to run the Akira ransomware payload in Safe Mode failed because the system reported low virtual memory and generated out-of-memory and PowerShell errors. Microsoft Defender later detected the Akira executable during a scheduled scan, but it only quarantined the file after the attacker rebooted the system into normal mode. Although encryption failed, the attacker still stole credentials and files for data extortion in less than five hours from initial access.

Drop Something? Don’t Worry, Someone Caught it

Infoblox found that about one in five newly registered domains are previously expired domains that have been re-registered, giving them inherited reputation, traffic, and lingering connections. This makes dropcatch domains attractive not only to investors and defenders, but also to threat actors who can abuse that residual trust for malware, hijacking, and other schemes.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Infoblox defines dropcatch domains as domains that expired, became available again, and were re-registered by someone else.
  • 02During the first half of 2026, Infoblox observed over 50,000 dropcatch domains per day in gTLDs alone and about 65,000 per day when including various ccTLDs.
  • 03Infoblox found that nearly 20% of observed daily gTLD registrations were dropcatch domains, meaning about one in five newly registered domains had a prior registration history.
  • 04Approximately 92% of all observed gTLD dropcatch domains came from just 15 TLDs, with .net and .xyz showing dropcatch rates of nearly three out of every ten newly observed domains.
  • 05The article says dropcatch domains can create security concerns because they may retain reputation, traffic, email, cached search results, lingering DNS records, and other connections from their previous owners.

Infoblox Threat Intel examined “dropcatch” domains, which are domains that expired, became available again, and were re-registered by someone else. During the first half of 2026, Infoblox observed over 50,000 dropcatch domains per day in gTLDs alone, rising to about 65,000 per day when including various ccTLDs. For gTLDs, nearly 20% of observed daily registrations were dropcatch domains, meaning about one in five newly registered domains had a prior life.

The article explains that dropped domains can come from failed businesses, missed renewal notices, abandoned internal domains, temporary events, charitable initiatives, political campaigns, personal blogs, mergers, acquisitions, and bulk registrations abandoned by threat actors. Measuring dropcatch activity is difficult because it depends on creation-date data and long-term domain history, and many ccTLD registries do not publicly provide creation dates. Infoblox focused on domains that reappeared with a new creation date after a prior registration, while domains that changed ownership before deletion were not included in its dataset.

The security significance is that re-registered domains may retain reputation, traffic, email, cached search results, old web references, and lingering DNS records from their previous owners. The article says this inherited trust can make such domains valuable to domain investors, defenders, and threat actors. Infoblox cites an example in which a previously expired CDN domain used by a marketing service was acquired in February 2026 by an actor it calls Shady Squirrel, who then began sending website visitors to malware.

  • A domain’s apparent age can be misleading because a re-registered domain may benefit from signals tied to its earlier life, causing researchers, security products, and reputation systems to view it more favorably than a truly new domain.
  • Creation-date availability strongly affects visibility into dropcatch activity, because gTLDs are easier to measure under ICANN registration data policies while many ccTLDs do not publicly provide creation dates.
  • Registrar and ownership data alone are often insufficient to determine whether a re-registered domain is being actively used, held for resale, parked, monetized, or controlled by a portfolio operator.
  • Expired domains can remain dangerous for years after abandonment because old links, embedded URLs, email flows, and DNS records may continue to point people or systems toward the domain after a new owner takes control.
  • The article’s CDN example shows that even domains tied to major media websites and acquired startups can be forgotten long enough for a later buyer to redirect visitors to malware.

The article explains that many web addresses expire and are quickly bought again by someone else; Infoblox saw about 65,000 of these reused addresses per day in early 2026. This affects businesses, charities, political campaigns, personal sites, and even large companies that may lose or abandon old web addresses, as well as people who still visit or send email to them. It matters because an old web address can still carry trust, visitors, email, and links from its past life, and the new owner could use that to mislead people or send them to harmful content.

Germany’s cabinet approved a major intelligence-law overhaul that would let the BND and BfV conduct hacking, sabotage, data interference and limited disinformation operations, while also imposing new oversight and restrictions including on AI analysis. The bill, driven by growing security threats, still needs parliamentary approval and is expected to face civil liberties challenges.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Germany’s cabinet approved draft legislation that would allow its intelligence agencies to hack foreign systems, sabotage adversaries’ supply chains, and feed false information to extremists inside Germany.
  • 02The bill would rewrite the laws governing Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, and its domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, and would require telecommunications carriers and digital service providers to assist the agencies when compelled.
  • 03The proposed powers would not allow measures intended to endanger a person’s life or physical safety, leaving the BND without paramilitary capabilities like those of some allied intelligence services.

Germany’s cabinet approved legislation that would let its intelligence agencies hack foreign systems, sabotage adversaries’ supply chains, and feed false information to extremists inside Germany. The bill would overhaul the laws governing the foreign intelligence service, the BND, and the domestic agency for the protection of the constitutional order, the BfV. It still has to clear parliament, but the governing coalition has said it wants the law in force next year.

Officials said the new powers could be used to substitute faulty components into deliveries, sabotage drone factories or chemical weapons laboratories through cyber operations, and disable servers run by hostile state-sponsored hackers and disinformation operators. The draft would also require telecommunications carriers and digital service providers to assist the agencies, with enforcement powers that could include fines or service suspension. The proposed powers stop short of allowing measures intended to endanger a person’s life or physical safety.

The bill would give the BfV new operational abilities, including blocking or rerouting data traffic, altering transmissions in transit, corrupting stored data used in a plot, and disabling equipment about to be used in an attack. It also authorizes self-learning systems for intelligence analysis while banning discriminatory algorithms and requiring spot checks of machine-generated outputs under the supervision of an officer qualified to serve as a judge. Civil liberties groups have said they plan to challenge the draft legislation.

  • The draft gives Germany’s domestic intelligence service an unusual power to feed false information to people inside the country, and the article states that no equivalent statutory authority exists in British, French, or American law.
  • Germany’s proposed framework is narrower than those of several close allies because it explicitly bars intelligence measures intended to endanger life or physical safety, rather than relying on broader legal authorizations for covert action abroad.
  • The bill treats some AI-generated conclusions, such as movement profiles and personality assessments, as intrusions in their own right, meaning the legal concern is not only the data collected but also what the system infers from it.
  • The legal rationale for the overhaul is complicated by a prior Constitutional Court judgment that allowed lower thresholds for intelligence agencies partly because they lacked operational powers, while the new bill would give them such powers.

Germany’s cabinet approved a proposed law that would give its foreign and domestic intelligence agencies new powers to break into foreign systems, disrupt hostile operations, interfere with data, and even feed false information to extremists inside Germany. Phone and digital service providers could be required to help, and people in Germany could be affected by the domestic agency’s new ability to alter or block communications linked to planned attacks. The issue matters because it would be the biggest change to Germany’s spy laws since the postwar era, expanding state power in a country especially sensitive to abuses by past secret police, while supporters say Germany faces growing threats from drones, terrorism, hostile states, and disinformation.

Microsoft patched the flaw in its July 2026 Patch Tuesday updates and said it stems from weak authentication. Successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication on a vulnerable SharePoint server and act as a SharePoint site user or administrator.

Rapid7 said the issue involves several weaknesses in the JWT token validation pipeline, specifically in two SharePoint classes that handle Bearer service-to-service tokens. The exploit chain can let an unauthenticated remote attacker forge a valid JWT and impersonate any SharePoint site user.

Rapid7’s Python-based proof of concept uses the forged JWT to query a target’s domain controller, enumerate users by SID, and locate a site administrator. One Extra Letter, Full Auth Pass, Nothing to Scan

Attackers impersonated a healthcare supplier using a one-letter typosquat domain that passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, then requested ACH banking details without using malicious links or payloads. The key lesson is that email authentication proves control of a domain, not legitimacy, so payment changes must be verified outside email.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A large U.S. regional healthcare system received an ACH enrolment notice from the typosquat domain arthrrex.com, which differed from the real medical-device manufacturer domain arthrex.com by one extra letter.
  • 02The attacker's domain had SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configured correctly, so the message passed email authentication checks under the attacker's own domain.
  • 03The attached PDF contained no JavaScript, form fields, embedded executable, account number, or routing details, and the email’s request to contact apinquiry@arthrrex.com was plain text rather than a link.
  • 04The PDF metadata showed it was created and modified on the same day the lookalike domain was registered, while the memo text was dated three days earlier.
  • 05IRONSCALES Themis scored the message at 84 percent confidence mainly because the return-path domain was newly registered, and four mailboxes across two waves were quarantined and mitigated.

A large U.S. regional healthcare system received an ACH enrolment notice that appeared to come from a medical-device manufacturer it already did business with. The sender used arthrrex[.]com, a one-character typosquat of the real arthrex[.]com domain with a doubled r. The message claimed the manufacturer was ending check and credit-card payments and moving payments to ACH through a subsidiary company under another name.

The email passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, Microsoft composite authentication, and ARC checks because the attacker owned and properly configured the lookalike domain. The links in the message pointed to the real manufacturer’s legitimate website and social channels, while the attached PDF had no JavaScript, form fields, embedded executable, account number, or routing details. The actual request was plain text asking recipients to email apinquiry@arthrrex[.]com with banking details, while the PDF said ACH information would arrive later as an encrypted file with a PIN sent separately.

The PDF metadata showed the memo was created and modified on the same day the typosquat domain was registered, despite the memo text being dated three days earlier. IRONSCALES Themis scored the message at 84 percent confidence because the return-path domain was newly registered, and four mailboxes across two waves were quarantined and mitigated. The article emphasizes that authentication checks only proved the attacker-controlled domain sent the email, and recommends treating payment-instruction changes as unverifiable by email and confirming them using contact information from the contract.

  • A full SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass can be misleading in business email compromise because it may only prove that the attacker controls the lookalike domain that sent the message.
  • The attacker avoided many gateway checks by putting the real request in plain text, using only clean links to the legitimate manufacturer’s public sites, and withholding bank details from the email and attachment.
  • Edit-distance checks against a company’s existing vendor list would have been more meaningful than generic domain reputation because the malicious domain differed from a real supplier’s domain by only one character.
  • The PDF’s metadata contradicted the memo’s printed date, showing that file metadata can expose a staged vendor-change narrative even when the attachment itself is not malicious.
  • Email-based verification is unsafe for payment-change requests in this scenario because the attacker designed the message to move the conversation into follow-up replies and out-of-band files.

A large U.S. healthcare system received an email that looked like it came from a medical-device manufacturer it already paid, asking it to switch payments to bank transfer. The sender used a nearly identical web address with one extra letter, so the email passed the usual checks even though it was controlled by the attacker. This matters because a company could be tricked into sending real money to the wrong bank account without any dangerous link or infected file to warn people. The article says payment changes should be confirmed using trusted contact details from the original contract, not by replying to the email.

  • 01Docker Sandboxes versions 0.35.0 through 0.37.1 had an issue where a directory mounted as read-only could still be written through another path.

Docker Sandboxes versions 0.35.0 through 0.37.1 had an oversight that allowed a directory mounted as read-only to be modified anyway. The issue was assigned CVE-2026-18171 with a CVSS score of 5.7, and Docker fixed it in version 0.38.0. The article explains that the impact depended on what the user mounted into the sandbox, such as source code, CI configuration, infrastructure code, application configuration, or build inputs.

The technical issue involved VirtioFS sharing host files with the sandbox microVM. A host directory mounted at a read-only path such as /readonly was also accessible through Docker’s host export under /mnt/host, where it remained writable. The article shows a proof of concept where writing to /readonly/file.txt failed, but writing to the same host file through /mnt/host/c/donotchangeme/file.txt succeeded and changed the file on the host.

  • The bypass was easy to discover from inside the sandbox because running findmnt exposed that /readonly was mounted read-only while /mnt/host was mounted writable.
  • The real-world risk was delayed execution: a malicious change to a build script or configuration file might only run later when a developer builds the project on the host or when CI processes the changed file.
  • The article emphasizes that sandbox strength depends heavily on boundary controls, because the testing assumed an agent had already followed malicious instructions and focused on whether it could reach beyond granted access.
  • Although the article reports a vulnerability, it also notes that other tested escape ideas failed because Docker Sandboxes' microVM, isolated Docker Engine, network controls, and credential proxy worked as intended.

The article explains that in certain versions of Docker Sandboxes, a folder that was supposed to be view-only could still be changed through another hidden path. This affects people using Docker Sandbox versions 0.35.0 through 0.37.1, especially if they let an AI coding tool inspect important files they did not want changed. In the real world, a compromised agent could quietly alter source code, build scripts, configuration, or other files that a developer or automated system later uses. Docker fixed the problem in version 0.38.0.

The article describes a proof-of-concept technique for turning Chromium-based browsers such as Chrome and Edge into a persistent command-and-control foothold by silently installing browser components. It focuses on SilentChrome-BOF, a Beacon object file that modifies Chromium profile state to install unpacked extensions, Isolated Web Applications, and Native Messaging Hosts. It also introduces Ditto, a Mythic agent that runs as a Chromium extension and can collect cookies, enumerate tabs, capture pages, query browser history, and communicate with optional sidecar components.

SilentChrome-BOF installs extensions by editing the profile’s Secure Preferences file, adding extension settings, enabling developer mode, recalculating protected preference MACs, removing encrypted hash entries, and recalculating the super_mac. The article explains that Chromium may accept the inserted extension when the legacy MACs match and the encrypted hash dictionary is removed, after which Chromium regenerates the encrypted hashes. It also explains that a reused manifest key can give a sideloaded extension the same extension ID as an existing published extension, which may bypass allowlists that trust extension IDs alone.

Ditto can be built with an Isolated Web Application for Direct Sockets-based SOCKS functionality and with a Native Messaging Host for selected Windows operating system actions through a local executable. The article recommends detections such as monitoring changes to Chromium Preferences and Secure Preferences files, registry creation or modification under NativeMessagingHosts, IWA-related Chrome command-line flags, and native messaging process launches containing chrome-extension origins. For prevention, the article says disabling extension developer mode with the ExtensionDeveloperModeSettings policy caused unpacked extensions to fail with DISABLE_UNSUPPORTED_DEVELOPER_EXTENSION.

  • Removing only the injected extension from Chromium’s encrypted hash dictionary was not sufficient; SilentChrome-BOF removes the entire `protection.macs.extensions.settings_encrypted_hash` dictionary so Chromium falls back to legacy MAC validation and regenerates the encrypted hashes itself.
  • Reusing the public key material from an already allowlisted Chrome Web Store extension can give a sideloaded extension the same extension ID, which may bypass enterprise allowlists that trust extension IDs alone.
  • Disabling extension developer mode with the mandatory `ExtensionDeveloperModeSettings` policy prevented the unpacked extension from starting because Chromium returned `DISABLE_UNSUPPORTED_DEVELOPER_EXTENSION`.
  • Native Messaging Host activity can expose the responsible browser extension because the native host process command line includes the connecting `chrome-extension://<extension-ID>` origin.
  • Launching Ditto’s IWA through the extension made Chromium process creation include IWA-related flags such as `--enable-isolated-web-apps-in-renderer` or `--enable-features=IsolatedWebApps`, giving defenders a concrete behavior to monitor.

The article explains a proof-of-concept way to quietly change Chrome or Edge user profile files so a hidden browser add-on can be installed and used to keep access, steal cookies, view browser data, and even interact with Windows through extra helper components. This affects people and organizations that use Chromium-based browsers like Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, especially where browser add-ons are trusted or allowed by policy. The broader risk is that the browser itself can become a long-lasting control point for an attacker, so defenders need to watch for unusual browser profile changes, new helper app registrations, and prevent unpacked add-ons from running.

In May 2026, Kaspersky discovered a new cyber-espionage campaign by Armored Likho, also known as Eagle Werewolf, targeting private individuals and organizations in Russia. The affected sectors include major corporations, the public sector, IT, and education. The campaign begins with a fake donation service app that appears legitimate while secretly decrypting and launching the next-stage payload.

The most significant finding is the Still Toolkit, a new Rust-based cyber-espionage toolkit made up of Still Sync and Still Audio. Still Sync steals Telegram session data and can use it to access the victim’s Telegram account through the Telegram API, collecting chats, media files, user details, and information about private chats, groups, and channels. Still Audio is an audio surveillance implant that detects speech, records conversations, encodes the recordings, and sends them to a command-and-control server.

Kaspersky attributes the campaign to Armored Likho with high confidence based on overlaps with earlier campaigns, including matching dropper architecture, shared sysmarker generation logic, reuse of an encryption algorithm and key, and similar infrastructure patterns. The attackers use domains and hosting providers that differ from the February campaign but follow similar naming patterns that mimic Windows system services and update mechanisms. Kaspersky says the new tools show the group is expanding its cyber-espionage capabilities into a cohesive tool ecosystem designed for long-term use and further expansion.

  • Still Audio uses a GitHub-hosted dead drop as a fallback for command-and-control information after three days of server unreachability, using the same Blowfish ECB encryption algorithm and key previously seen in AquilaRAT.
  • The audio implant does not fully hide its microphone use from Windows settings; in the analyzed sample, IntAudio.exe appeared as “Intel Audio” in the list of apps using the microphone.
  • The attackers’ infrastructure avoids direct domain and IP overlap with the February campaign but still reuses hosting-provider choices and Windows-service-like domain naming patterns, which Kaspersky cites as part of the attribution picture.

Check Point Research’s State of Ransomware Q2 2026 report says the ransomware ecosystem is starting to shift after a period dominated by a handful of large RaaS operations. The leaders are still responsible for much of the damage, but the path to becoming a major operator has become shorter. The top 10 groups accounted for 57.6% of victims, down from 71% in Q1, while active groups rose from 71 to 93.

Victim volume remained high, with data leak sites recording 2,139 victims in Q2, essentially flat from Q1 and up 33% year over year. Qilin stayed the most prolific operator for a fourth straight quarter with 279 victims, though its count fell 17%. The Gentlemen rose 62% to 269 victims and outpaced Qilin during June.

The report highlights an internal leak from The Gentlemen that exposed a core team of about nine operators, a broader affiliate base, and use of AI coding assistants to build a ransomware management panel in about three days. Ransom payment rates fell to a multi-year low near 23%, even as on-chain ransomware payments exceeded $820 million in 2025 and average and median payments moved in different directions. Law enforcement focused on shared infrastructure used by multiple ransomware actors, while the US share of victims fell from 50% to 42% and vulnerabilities continued to be weaponized within hours to days of disclosure.

  • Law enforcement in Q2 focused on services used across multiple ransomware groups, such as laundering, malware signing, infostealer, and anonymization infrastructure, rather than only pursuing individual ransomware brands.
  • The drop in the US victim share from 50% to 42% shows that changes in which groups grow fastest can meaningfully shift the geographic distribution of ransomware impact.
  • The payment market is splitting: fewer victims are paying overall, but large enterprises continue to make high payments while the mid-market increasingly refuses or settles for smaller amounts.

A new Check Point Research report says ransomware activity stayed very high in Q2 2026, but the field is changing: the biggest groups still caused much of the harm, while many more smaller groups became active. Cisco Talos identified an undocumented phishing framework internally branded “JWR” that impersonates checkout and login pages across major payment and shopping platforms. The framework can harvest complete payment card data, login credentials, personally identifiable information, identity document images, 2FA codes, and device fingerprints in real time. Talos assesses with medium confidence that JWR is a variant of “The Outsider,” a phishing-as-a-service platform, based on similarities in client engine scripts and functionality.

The JWR client engine uses a real-time, operator-driven design rather than simply collecting submitted form data. It keeps an AES-CTR encrypted WebSocket open to the actor’s command-and-control server, allowing the operator to steer the victim’s session live, redirect them between phishing pages, display fake errors, and request additional information such as OTPs, PINs, or app approvals. The Vue.js victim application renders across 44 phishing pages, streams keystrokes as they are typed, and supports more than 40 actor-issued instructions.

Talos observed an active SMS phishing campaign delivering the JWR client through lures impersonating toll authorities, postal services, and courier services in Southeast Asia and the Middle East. The malicious URLs led victims to fake pages that loaded the JWR client and enabled host mode. The article also notes JWR integrations for Shopify and WooCommerce, which can reconstruct realistic shopping cart details to make fake checkout pages more convincing.

  • JWR streams victim keystrokes to the operator as they are typed, allowing the actor to decide the next fake verification step before the victim submits the form.
  • The framework can repeatedly show fake failure prompts such as declined-card or invalid-code messages, enabling the operator to pressure one victim into entering multiple cards or verification codes in a single session.
  • JWR includes an HTTP long-poll fallback endpoint for environments where WebSocket connections are blocked, preserving live operator control under more restrictive network conditions.
  • The client stores and reuses a JWRCID session token across visits, allowing the operator to correlate repeat visits from the same device.
  • JWR’s Shopify and WooCommerce integrations reconstruct realistic cart details such as product names, quantities, prices, and totals, making the fake checkout flow more convincing.

Cisco Talos found a phishing tool called JWR that creates fake checkout and login pages for services like Shopify, PayPal, Apple, Klarna, and banks, while letting the scammer guide each victim through the fake site in real time. People who click scam text messages about tolls, postal fees, or courier deliveries can be tricked into giving up far more than card numbers, including passwords, identity documents, Social Security numbers, one-time codes, and device details. Talos saw this being used in campaigns impersonating toll, postal, and courier services in Southeast Asia and the Middle East, showing how these scams can be run across many countries and brands at scale.

The article says that position could allow policy changes, certificate and key access, log manipulation, and visibility into inspected traffic. Fortinet rates the issue High, while third-party trackers report a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8, with the article noting that defenders should judge risk based on whether their appliances use the affected configuration.

Fortinet lists FortiWeb 8.0, 7.6, 7.4, 7.2, and 7.0 branches as affected, but the article stresses that risk is narrower than the version list because it depends on use of remote RADIUS administrator authentication through an admin group. No public proof of concept has been reported, and Fortinet has not reported exploitation in the wild at the time of writing. Until fixed versions are confirmed, the article recommends inventorying FortiWeb appliances, identifying those using RADIUS admin authentication, restricting management access, disabling RADIUS-based admin groups where local accounts are sufficient, and auditing administrator activity.

  • The article emphasizes that the real priority should be determined by whether each FortiWeb appliance uses RADIUS-backed administrator groups, not by the broad list of affected software versions or the highest published severity score.
  • Patch status is ambiguous enough that the article advises defenders to confirm fixed builds directly with Fortinet instead of assuming that versions beyond third-party affected ranges are safe.
  • CyCognito’s exposure data identifies FortiWeb assets through service fingerprinting but does not confirm software version or administrator authentication configuration, so the observed assets are potentially affected rather than confirmed vulnerable.
  • The article highlights a security paradox: FortiWeb appliances are deployed to protect edge web applications, but if their own management login path is exposed and vulnerable, that protective position can become a high-value entry point.

Fortinet disclosed a FortiWeb flaw, CVE-2026-26035, that can let someone log in as an administrator without valid credentials when the appliance is set up to use RADIUS admin groups. The affected systems are FortiWeb web application firewalls in several software branches, especially those using this central login setup rather than only local administrator accounts. This matters because FortiWeb often sits at the edge of an organization in front of important websites and APIs, and an intruder with administrator access could change protections, view inspected traffic, access certificates and keys, or hide signs of activity.

It is broadly relevant to security teams because exploitation could grant full appliance control, but the article notes no public proof of concept or in-the-wild exploitation at the time of writing.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-71362) Adobe Commerce Account Takeover via Session Identity Flaw

Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source have a critical unauthenticated account-takeover flaw, CVE-2026-71362, affecting public storefronts on multiple 2.4.x release lines. Fixed August 2026 patches are available, but organizations should urgently inventory all storefronts, including staging and campaign sites, patch, invalidate sessions, and monitor for exploitation.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-71362 is a critical incorrect authorization vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to switch an active session to a different customer account.
  • 02Affected software includes Adobe Commerce 2.4.4 through 2.4.9 and Magento Open Source 2.4.6 through 2.4.9 at the 2026-jul build and earlier in each line.
  • 03Adobe published fixed 2026-aug builds in bulletin APSB26-92 on August 11, 2026, covering Adobe Commerce, Magento Open Source, and Adobe Commerce B2B supported lines.
  • 04Adobe says it is not aware of exploitation in the wild, while Sansec reports that its Shield web application firewall is already blocking exploitation attempts against this CVE.
  • 05The article recommends inventorying all Adobe Commerce and Magento hosts, deploying WAF coverage for storefront customer and session endpoints, invalidating active customer sessions after patching, monitoring logs for account or session switching, and scanning exposed stores for backdoors.

CVE-2026-71362 is a critical incorrect authorization vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source with a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.1. The flaw is caused by the platform failing to correctly bind a customer identity to an account session. Adobe says exploitation requires no authentication, no administrator privileges, and no user interaction, with only network access to the public storefront required.

Sansec’s patch analysis found that the issue involves improper handling of customer identity within an account session, allowing an attacker to switch an active session to a different customer account. In practice, this gives the attacker that customer’s authenticated context, including access to stored personal data and order history. Adobe says it is not aware of exploits in the wild, while Sansec reports that its Shield web application firewall is already blocking exploitation attempts against this CVE.

Affected assets include Adobe Commerce 2.4.4 through 2.4.9 and Magento Open Source 2.4.6 through 2.4.9 at the 2026-jul build and earlier, with Adobe Commerce B2B fixes also included in the same bulletin. Adobe published fixed 2026-aug builds in APSB26-92 on August 11, 2026, but the article notes that isolated patches may require stores to already be on the latest point release for their supported branch. Recommended actions include inventorying all Adobe Commerce and Magento hosts, deploying WAF coverage for storefront customer and session endpoints, invalidating active customer sessions after patching, monitoring for account or session switching, and scanning exposed stores for backdoors.

  • The article highlights a meaningful discrepancy in exploitation status: Adobe says it is not aware of in-the-wild exploitation, but Sansec reports its WAF is already blocking attempts, so defenders should verify their own exposure rather than relying only on the vendor advisory.
  • Remediation may take longer than simply applying the August fix because Adobe’s monthly fixes are distributed as isolated patches and require stores to already be on the latest point release for their supported branch.
  • The highest exposure concentration in the observed dataset is in Communication Services, where many small, separately managed merchandise, ticketing, licensing, and promotional storefronts can create a fragmented patching problem.
  • The article emphasizes that staging, preproduction, UAT, developer, and campaign storefronts are part of the real exposure surface because they often run the same codebase but may be excluded from normal production change control.
  • Session invalidation after patching is specifically recommended because the flaw involves improper handling of customer identity inside active account sessions.

The article describes a critical flaw in Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source that can let someone with only internet access take over a shopper’s account on an affected online store. It affects public storefronts running certain older 2.4.x versions, including production, staging, campaign, and other overlooked sites. This matters because an attacker could see a customer’s personal details and order history, and many organizations may not even know all the stores they still have online.

The article also notes conflicting exploit status, with Adobe saying it is unaware of exploitation while Sansec reports blocking exploitation attempts.

Potential for Remote Code Execution in Microsoft SCCM via Newly-Discovered Exploit Chain

XM Cyber researchers found an SCCM exploit chain that can let a low-privileged domain user or Operations Administrator achieve remote code execution as SYSTEM on the primary site server. Microsoft has patched only the RBAC bypass so far, leaving parts of the chain unpatched until a planned future ConfigMgr release, so organizations should restrict AdminService access and audit SCCM roles.
KEY POINTS
  • 01XM Cyber researchers discovered a chain of vulnerabilities in Microsoft System Center Configuration Management that could allow remote code execution by a standard domain user with no SCCM permissions, no admin role, and no user interaction.
  • 02Microsoft assigned CVE-2026-47301 to one vulnerability in the chain and released a July 2026 fix for the broken authorization issue, but the article states that the rest of the chain remains unpatched until a planned ConfigMgr 2609 release in October 2026.
  • 03The exploit chain combines a missing authorization check in an AdminService chunked upload endpoint, weak code-signing verification, a path traversal issue in CAB extraction called “CabSlip,” and unsigned secondary DLL loading by SMS Executive.
  • 04The same downstream exploit path can still be triggered by SCCM users with the built-in Operations Administrator role or any custom role with Create permission on the SMS_ConsoleExtensionData object type.
  • 05The article recommends monitoring AdminService.log for a System.IO.DirectoryNotFoundException followed by an HTTP 500 response, watching for unexpected changes to adsource.dll, restricting network access to the AdminService API port, and auditing SCCM role assignments.

XM Cyber researchers discovered a chain of vulnerabilities in Microsoft System Center Configuration Management that could be used to achieve remote code execution. The article says a standard domain user with no SCCM permissions, no admin role, and no user interaction could take advantage of the chain. The exploit targets the primary site server, which manages the entire infrastructure, and successful exploitation could grant control over the whole environment.

Microsoft assigned CVE-2026-47301 to one vulnerability in the chain and released a fix for that issue in July 2026. The article states that the rest of the chain remains unpatched, with Microsoft planning fixes in ConfigMgr 2609 in October 2026. SCCM is widely used for operating system deployment, patch management, software distribution, and compliance monitoring, and the article cites Microsoft reports of more than 100 million active users.

The chain combines a missing authorization check in an AdminService upload endpoint, weak code-signing verification, a CAB extraction path traversal issue called “CabSlip,” and automatic privileged DLL loading by SMS Executive. Even after the authorization fix, users with the Operations Administrator role or Create permission on SMS_ConsoleExtensionData can still trigger the downstream chain through a different API. The article recommends monitoring AdminService.log for a System.IO.DirectoryNotFoundException followed by an HTTP 500 response, watching for unexpected changes to adsource.dll, restricting network access to the AdminService API port, and auditing SCCM role assignments.

  • The July 2026 fix changes the immediate risk profile: standard domain users are blocked from abusing the chunked upload endpoint, but users with the built-in Operations Administrator role can still reach the same downstream code execution path through a different upload API.
  • The code-signing check described in the article is weak enough that SCCM accepts a CAB signed with any standard commercially purchased code-signing certificate, rather than requiring a Microsoft or organization-specific trusted signer.
  • A failed cleanup operation can become a practical detection signal because the path traversal causes extracted files to land outside the expected ExpandedCab folder, leading to a System.IO.DirectoryNotFoundException followed by an HTTP 500 error in AdminService.log.
  • Microsoft does not support disabling SCCMProviderGraph.exe, so the article’s recommended mitigation before the full vendor fix is to restrict network access to the AdminService API port instead.
  • The article highlights a specific high-value file integrity target, adsource.dll, because overwriting it can lead SMS Executive to load attacker-controlled code as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.

Researchers at XM Cyber found a way to abuse weaknesses in Microsoft SCCM, a widely used tool that helps organizations manage and update large numbers of Windows computers. In some cases, even a regular company network account with no special SCCM rights could use the chain to take control of the main SCCM server, and Microsoft says more than 100 million people use the service. Microsoft fixed one part of the problem, but the article says the rest is still unpatched until a planned later release, so companies using SCCM may remain at risk.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

It is broadly relevant because Microsoft has patched only one part of the chain and the article states that remaining issues are still unpatched pending a future ConfigMgr release.

Team PCP Stole 78,330 Secrets From 2,186 Organizations. CloudSEK Just Published the List.

Team PCP allegedly stole 78,330 secrets from CI/CD pipelines across 2,186 organizations by compromising trusted open source components and using them to harvest credentials at scale. The key takeaway is that CI/CD systems are now a primary supply-chain target and need production-grade controls like dependency pinning, runtime monitoring, and network egress restrictions.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CloudSEK published a searchable dataset showing that Team PCP exfiltrated 78,330 distinct secrets from the CI/CD pipelines of 2,186 organizations between March 19 and March 24, 2026.
  • 02The article says Team PCP’s playbook is to compromise trusted open source components, run credential stealers in CI/CD pipelines, exfiltrate secrets, and use those credentials to compromise additional maintainers, repositories, or registries.
  • 03StepSecurity’s analysis of the CloudSEK dataset found affected organizations using GitLab, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Jenkins, Bitbucket Pipelines, and CircleCI, with GitLab accounting for 1,064 exposed organizations.
  • 04The exposed credentials included JWTs, private key blocks, AWS access keys, GitLab personal access tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, OpenAI keys, Slack webhooks, and Google API keys.
  • 05The article recommends that organizations appearing in the dataset rotate exposed credentials, audit access logs since March 19, 2026, pin CI/CD dependencies to immutable references, and deploy runtime and network egress controls on runners.

Team PCP exfiltrated 78,330 distinct secrets from the CI/CD pipelines of 2,186 organizations over five days, from March 19 to 24, 2026. CloudSEK published a searchable dataset of the exposure, and StepSecurity analyzed it. The affected organizations include 92 public companies with a combined market capitalization above $6.2 trillion.

The article describes Team PCP as a threat actor that compromises trusted open source projects, plants credential stealers, collects secrets from CI/CD runners, and uses stolen credentials to compromise additional maintainers, repositories, or registries. The campaign included compromises involving the Trivy GitHub Action, the Checkmarx KICS action, the telnyx PyPI package, and LiteLLM. StepSecurity’s analysis found that GitLab accounted for 1,064 exposed organizations, followed by GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Jenkins, Bitbucket Pipelines, and CircleCI.

The stolen secrets included JWTs, private key blocks, AWS access keys, GitLab and GitHub personal access tokens, OpenAI keys, Slack webhooks, and Google API keys. The article argues that CI/CD pipelines are being targeted because they often hold powerful credentials while lacking controls such as runtime monitoring, network egress restrictions, and governance over which dependencies execute with secrets in scope. It recommends that affected organizations rotate exposed credentials, audit access logs since March 19, 2026, pin CI/CD dependencies to immutable references, and deploy runtime and network egress controls on runners.

  • The campaign was not mainly a GitHub Actions problem: StepSecurity’s analysis found GitLab had the most exposed organizations by a wide margin, and Azure DevOps appeared in more than 230 organizations.
  • The article emphasizes that rotating exposed credentials is not sufficient because the dataset shows what left the runners, not what Team PCP may already have done with the stolen access.
  • A single compromised open source component can expose many organizations at once because CI/CD pipelines often load secrets into environments where any running step can read them.
  • The presence of 157 leaked OpenAI API keys and the LiteLLM compromise led CloudSEK to frame the incident as an AI supply chain event, showing that AI infrastructure is being affected through ordinary software delivery pipelines.
  • The article argues that pinning dependencies only closes one route of compromise because Team PCP also reached runners through dependencies that were not known to be compromised at the time.

The article says a group called Team PCP stole 78,330 secret keys and tokens from the software-building systems of 2,186 organizations in five days by first compromising trusted open source projects that many companies use. The affected organizations include companies using GitLab, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Jenkins, Bitbucket Pipelines, and CircleCI, including 92 public companies worth a combined $6.2 trillion. This matters because those stolen secrets can let attackers enter company systems, cloud accounts, code repositories, and other services, and then use that access to compromise more software projects.

The article includes concrete impact details, affected technology ecosystems, and immediate response steps for potentially exposed organizations.
