PATCHCORD: New malware cluster targets Afghan telecom and South Asian critical infrastructure

Acronis researchers uncovered an active espionage campaign using new PATCHCORD, SHEETCORD, and HACKERAI implants to target Afghan telecom providers and South Asian government, defense, and critical infrastructure organizations. The activity is assessed with moderate confidence to overlap with APT36/Transparent Tribe and uses evolving C2 methods including custom HTTP, Google Sheets, and GitHub Gists.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Acronis Threat Research Unit identified an ongoing campaign delivering a previously undocumented C/C++ backdoor called PATCHCORD against Afghan telecom providers and South Asian critical infrastructure organizations.
  • 02PATCHCORD was delivered through sector-specific lures, including a fake Afghan Telecom TMS installer, and it communicates with the hardcoded C2 domain appstoore[.]solutions over TCP port 8080.
  • 03Infrastructure pivoting uncovered SHEETCORD, a Go-based implant distributed through a domain impersonating India’s National Informatics Centre and using Google Sheets for command-and-control communication.
  • 04An exposed staging server tied to the campaign contained campaign files, SuperShell C2 framework, multiple RAT frameworks, credential harvesting tools, and exploit tooling for CVE-2024-6387 and CVE-2021-4034.
  • 05Acronis assesses with moderate confidence that the campaign overlaps with APT36, also known as Transparent Tribe, based on targeting patterns, malware similarities, shared infrastructure, and operational tradecraft.

Acronis Threat Research Unit identified an ongoing campaign delivering a previously undocumented custom backdoor called PATCHCORD against Afghan telecom providers and South Asian critical infrastructure organizations. The malware was delivered through sector-specific lures, including fake VPN installers impersonating Afghan Telecom and telecom management tools. Infrastructure pivoting also uncovered SHEETCORD, a Go-based implant that builds on PATCHCORD’s capabilities while abusing Google Sheets for command-and-control communication, and HACKERAI C2 Agent, which uses GitHub Gists for tasking and data exfiltration.

The campaign’s infrastructure centers on a single C2 server at 46.30.188.13 with multiple associated domains impersonating Afghan telecom operators, Indian government entities, and other organizations. Acronis found that the same infrastructure served additional campaigns, including one impersonating India’s National Informatics Centre to distribute SHEETCORD and an earlier campaign targeting India’s energy sector with a PATCHCORD variant. TRU assesses with moderate confidence that the activity overlaps with APT36, also known as Transparent Tribe, based on targeting patterns, malware similarities, shared infrastructure, and operational tradecraft.

PATCHCORD establishes persistence through browser shortcut hijacking and a registry Run key, fingerprints the host, registers with its C2 server, and supports process enumeration, in-memory shellcode execution, remote command execution, and control over the shortcut hijacking mechanism. SHEETCORD reimplements similar browser shortcut hijacking, adds startup persistence through a VBScript file and registry Run key, and uses Google Sheets API v4 with hardcoded GCP service account credentials for victim-specific communication. An exposed staging server revealed campaign lures, SuperShell C2 framework, GateSentinel, HackBrowserData, Metasploit artifacts, credential brute-forcing files, and exploit tooling for CVE-2024-6387 and CVE-2021-4034.

  • PATCHCORD preserves the user’s normal browser experience after hijacking browser shortcuts by silently launching the legitimate browser first, making the persistence mechanism less noticeable to victims.
  • The same operator infrastructure supported three distinct command-and-control methods across related implants: PATCHCORD used a custom HTTP server, SHEETCORD abused Google Sheets, and HACKERAI C2 Agent used GitHub Gists.
  • The exposed staging server showed that campaign files for Afghan telecom lures were stored alongside tools such as SuperShell, GateSentinel, HackBrowserData, Metasploit, and CVE-2024-6387 exploit tooling, giving defenders concrete clues about the operator’s broader toolkit.
  • The threat actor maintained a single C2 server at 46.30.188.13 while rotating many impersonation domains over several months, so blocking or investigating only one domain may miss related active infrastructure.
  • The SHEETCORD implant expanded PATCHCORD’s browser shortcut hijacking from three browsers to six, adding Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi in addition to Chrome, Firefox, and Edge.

Acronis researchers found an active spying campaign using newly documented harmful programs called PATCHCORD, SHEETCORD, and HACKERAI against Afghan telecom providers and government, defense, energy, and other critical organizations in South Asia. The attackers used fake installers that looked like Afghan Telecom, India’s National Informatics Centre, and other trusted organizations to trick people into running them. This matters because telecom providers can give spies access to communications infrastructure, subscriber information, and government communications, so a compromise could affect far more than one company.
